title: nvprof-to-nsight-transition-microbatch-timeline-case-notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working note capturing the results from switching a set of microbatch-focused profiling runs from nvprof sampling to full Nsight timeline capture. The goal was to reproduce an intermittent tail-latency spike we've been seeing in production during 8-12 token generation windows (microbatch size 1-4), and to understand whether kernel launch pacing, async memcpy timing, or NVLink peer-to-peer saturation is the root cause.

Motivation / Background:
- Production symptom: occasional 95th/99th token latency spikes (+120–300 ms) on a subset of 80B-ish models when handling many short requests concurrently.
- Previous sampling runs (nvprof) pointed at elevated memcpy times and sporadic kernel queue gaps, but nvprof sampling resolution and lack of full timeline made it hard to spot causal ordering.
- Plan: capture full Nsight timeline with NVTX markers on the runtime handoff points (batcher->executor, prefetch start/end, kv-cache hit sequences) and compare with equivalent nvprof counters to reconcile differences.

Experiment setup:
- Hosts: r5g.8x-like instance with 8x A100-80GB (NVLink stitched) in our staging cluster.
- Model: quantized-decoder-77B-v2 (serving build: runtime-1.14.3).
- Workload: synthetic microbatch load generator (tool: bench-gen v0.9) producing poisson arrivals targeted to 1200 RPS aggregate across 4 GPUs. Request lengths: 8–12 tokens.
- Profiles collected: Nsight Systems 2025.3 timeline (10s captures), nvprof 2024 sampling runs (for counter baselines), and per-request logs from runtime with NVTX markers.
- Capture flags: nsight --trace=cuda,nvtx,cudnn --capture-range=cudaProfilerStart/cudaProfilerStop; include stream names and kernel symbols.

Key NVTX markers used (inserted in code):
- NVTX_BATCHER_HANDFOFF_START / _END
- NVTX_PREFETCH_START / _END
- NVTX_KERNEL_DISPATCH / _COMPLETE (per kernel region)
- NVTX_KV_CACHE_LOOKUP_START / _END

Trace excerpts (high-level, paraphrased):
- Example timeline slice (t=37.42s): batcher handoff -> 1.2ms gap -> prefetch async memcpy start -> 32us async memcpy -> kernel dispatch (persistent kernel small setup) -> kernel runs 0.8ms -> synchronous stream wait for kv-cache miss -> follow-up kernel 1.4ms -> host copy back 48us -> final send.
- Example anomalous slice (t=112.7s): batcher handoff -> 18.7ms gap (no CUDA activity on primary stream) -> prefetch memcpy shows repeated short async memcpy bursts on peer stream -> a kernel launches but is queued behind a long-running kernel on another stream (different CU occupancy) -> subsequent kv-cache lookup stalls 9–14ms while persistent kernel is preempted.

Observations:
1) The Nsight timeline shows that the majority of the large spikes correlate with scheduling holes between Batcher_Handoff_END and PREFETCH_START. Those holes are 10–40ms in bad slices.
2) Nvprof sampling did not always show the holes because it aggregated kernel times and memcpy counters; short idle windows were smoothed out by sampling.
3) We frequently saw small repeated async memcpy bursts (~20–200 us) on peer streams (for NVLink transfers) that precede the gap. Hypothesis: these bursts cause transient congestion on the NVLink scheduler or DMA engines, producing delay before the main prefetch memcpy on the GPU that the request relies on.
4) Kernel preemption/serialization: some persistent kernels (e.g., kv-cache scanners) are long-lived on their streams and intermittently block higher-priority dispatches on other streams due to shared SM scheduling and CTA placement. The timeline shows overlap and partial blocking that nvprof counters treated as serialized time.
5) Stream priority didn't fully explain the delay. We tested priority promotion on the prefetch stream and saw reduced but not eliminated spikes — suggests contention is at a lower layer (DMA engine or NVLink).

Hypotheses (ranked):
- H1 (high): NVLink/DMA micro-bursts from prefetch/peer activities create transient backpressure affecting subsequent async memcpy latency for the request, leading to holes in the primary execution timeline.
- H2 (medium): Persistent kernels with poor CTA affinity cause SM-level interference that delays small short-lived kernels due to warp scheduling starvation.
- H3 (low): Host-side queuing and context-switch jitter (kernel launch pacing) contributes, but only amplifies rather than primary cause.

Small experiments run and quick results:
- Stream priority promotion (raise prefetch stream priority): 30% drop in observed spikes in synthetic run, but some 95th latencies persisted.
- Co-locating prefetch memcpys to a single designated peer stream (serialize peer copies): eliminated the async-memcpy-burst pattern and reduced holes, but increased aggregate memcpy tail slightly.
- Reducing persistent kernel residency (split long kernels into shorter checkpoints): removed many examples of queued prefetch kernels but added a small scheduling overhead; net win for tail latency in microbatch regime.
- NVLink stress test (separate tool to saturate links): when NVLink saturated, gaps increase proportionally; suggests link saturation compounds the problem.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- We need a lower-level trace that correlates DMA engine queues and NVLink FLIT-level stats with CUDA timeline; is that possible with our Nsight build or driver level telemetry?
- Is there a kernel placement heuristic (launcher-side) we can adopt to avoid CTA placement collisions between long-lived persistent kernels and short ephemeral kernels?
- Should we introduce an internal prefetch-rate limiter to smooth peer-copy bursts? Trade-off: added latency vs reduced tail spikes.

Immediate action items (owners + rough ETA):
- Aisha: prototype a prefetch-rate limiter that batches peer copies into a short-leaky-bucket (ETA: 2026-03-25).
- Samir: instrument the persistent-kernel launcher to try a lightweight CTA-affinity seeding heuristic in staging (ETA: 2026-03-22).
- Marco (me): run NVLink telemetry experiment with driver debug flags and capture a 30s Nsight run under saturated and unsaturated conditions (ETA: 2026-03-20).
- Lena: validate production traces (s3 bucket logs) for the 8–12 token request traces and tag suspicious slices for later cross-correlation (ETA: 2026-03-21).

Longer term options to consider:
- Kernel preemption-friendly designs: move long-running maintenance kernels to time-sliced mode or cooperative-yield variants so short kernels can execute quickly.
- Scheduler-level backpressure awareness: implement a runtime-level NVLink/DMA budgeter that spreads out peer copies if the link is near-saturated.
- Explore hardware-backed QoS (if available) for NVLink or DMA channels — talk to infra / cloud vendor.

Appendix A — useful commands and capture notes:
- Nsight capture example: nsys profile --force-overwrite true --capture-range cudaProfilerStart,cudaProfilerStop --output nsight/microbatch-2026-03-10 --trace=cuda,nvtx,cudnn --sample=none --capture-on-start false --stop-on-exit true 
- To convert: nsys export --input nsight/microbatch-2026-03-10.qdrep --output timeline/microbatch-2026-03-10.json --format json
- NVTX tips: ensure markers include a monotonically increasing id for request correlation; sync points are expensive in timeline capture, prefer many small markers rather than coarse-grained ones to pinpoint gaps.

Appendix B — quick checklist for future captures:
- Enable stream names and include NVTX request ids.
- Run capture on warm GPU to avoid outliers from GPU wake-up.
- Run paired captures: with/without peer-copy serialization to isolate NVLink effects.

Notes to self:
- This feels like the right path; nvprof sampling gave us hints but Nsight timeline provided the causal ordering. Focus next on correlating DMA/NVLink telemetry and test the prefetch-rate limiter in staging.

---
